title: Redwood Discovery - Model Selection (AzureWave AI)
summary: Intro discovery focused on model selection for multilingual customer-facing features. Discussed tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments; context length requirements (~32k tokens), tool-calling, and security needs (SOC2, KMS, SSO). Agreed next steps: share benchmark spreadsheet, SOC2/KMS docs, schedule SE-led benchmark with customer data.
topics: deployment mode: hosted vs dedicated vs private
next_steps: Maya to run shortlist benchmark on sample dataset and share results by 2027-07-26
Sanjay to send pricing estimate for Dedicated (2x GPU) and Hosted options by 2027-07-24
Priya to review SOC2 and KMS docs once shared
Schedule technical deep-dive benchmark week of 2027-07-26
action_items: Maya Chen - run model comparison (LLama-2 variants, Mistral, Mistral-instruct, Redwood-verified open models) on sample multilingual dataset - due 2027-07-26
Marcus Ng - upload 5k labeled examples and typical long-form documents, and share seq length distribution - due 2027-07-25
Sanjay Patel - send SOC2 summary, KMS integration notes, and initial pricing spreadsheet - due 2027-07-24
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-07-23 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~45 minutes | Attendees: Sanjay Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Lena Torres (CTO - AzureWave AI), Marcus Ng (ML Platform), Priya Desai (Security)

[00:00:00] Sanjay: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro — I'm Sanjay, AE on the account, and Maya is our SE. we wanted to run through your model selection needs and figure out whether Hosted, Dedicated or Private is the right fit.

[00:00:18] Lena: thanks, sanjay. we appreciate the time. high level — we're building a customer support assistant that needs to be multilingual, and some workflows call out to internal tools (so tool-calling / function calling is important). also we expect pretty long contexts, roughly 20k to 32k tokens for full conversation + docs.

[00:00:40] Maya: great — that helps. quick clarifying q: when you say tool-calling, is that server-side function calls, or do you mean external APIs and RAG-style retrieval?

[00:00:50] Marcus: both, actually. primary is function calls to our internal ticketing system for triage, and secondary is retrieval-augmented generation pulling long docs. we want deterministic structured outputs for some calls.

[00:01:05] Priya: from security side, we need SOC2 and SSO (SAML) + customer-managed KMS for key control if we go private. data residency is also a potential ask — europe-first.

[00:01:20] Sanjay: totally — Redwood supports SAML/SSO, RBAC, and for Private deployments we can integrate with customer KMS/HSM. We'll share our SOC2 docs. For Hosted we have encryption at rest, but if you need customer-managed keys, Dedicated or Private is the path.

[00:01:37] Lena: good to know. on models — we're evaluating open models for cost reasons. Multilingual quality is top priority, then latency and cost. do you have recommended families for 32k contexts and tool-calling?

[00:01:53] Maya: short answer: depends. for 32k context lengths you want models trained or fine-tuned for long context — some open families like LLama-2 xlong variants and a few Mistral forks handle extended context but with tradeoffs. Redwood also offers verified model profiles that show memory & latency. If you need function-calling reliability and structured outputs, model finetuning + instruction-tuning helps.

[00:02:15] Marcus: can you be specific — llm vendors are throwing terms around. which models would you shortlist for us?

[00:02:23] Maya: our typical shortlist for multilingual + long context is: LLama-2-70b-xlong (quantized variants), Mistral-extended (community forks), and a couple smaller 32k-optimized models like 'Redwood-verified xlang-32k' (internal naming), plus we sometimes recommend a mid-size 30b family for latency sensitivity. We also propose a two-model strategy: a bigger long-context model for full doc reasoning, and a smaller fast model for short replies.

[00:02:49] Lena: the two-model approach sounds interesting — complexity for ops?

[00:02:54] Sanjay: it's manageable. Redwood's routing lets you split by policy — route long-doc requests to the large 32k model and quick UI responses to the faster small model. You can also fallback if the big model is busy.

[00:03:10] Priya: what about hallucination and tool-calling safety? we need safe defaults and to ensure function-calls don't leak creds.

[00:03:18] Maya: function-calling safety is mostly about system design — we suggest policy layers, validation, and a strict schema for function outputs. Redwood supports structured response enforcement and schema validation; SE can show examples. Regarding hallucination, model choice + prompt engineering + RAG with trusted docs reduce risk.

[00:03:37] Marcus: ok. cost — if we pick the long-context 70b model, are we looking at Dedicated only? Hosted is cheaper to try out, right?

[00:03:46] Sanjay: Hosted is fastest to get started and good for evaluation — you pay per token. For predictable throughput at scale and compliance isolation, Dedicated is common. Private is for stricter security / on-prem requirements. There's a cost curve: Hosted per-token, Dedicated reserved capacity (monthly commit), Private has platform fee + infra. We'll send a pricing comparison.

[00:04:05] Lena: our timeline — pilot in August, production H2. Need to know latency SLOs — sub-second for small replies, under 3s for typical queries.

[00:04:14] Maya: got it. small replies sub-second is achievable with mid-size quantized models on Dedicated or optimized Hosted paths with lower batch sizes. For 32k contexts the per-token latency increases; kernel selection and KV cache matter.

[00:04:30] Marcus: KV cache? can you explain briefly?

[00:04:33] Maya: sure — in long-context workloads we keep key-value caches for previous tokens to avoid recomputing. Redwood's runtime manages KV cache across requests and can do prefix caching for repeated documents to reduce compute. That helps latency and cost on long sessions.

[00:04:48] Priya: international data residency — we prefer EU-only for EU customers. Does Redwood Hosted allow region-specific tenancy?

[00:04:55] Sanjay: yes, we have region routing and EU hosted regions. For stricter compliance, Dedicated in EU or Private in your VPC is the recommended path.

[00:05:05] Lena: fine. what about multilingual quality — do you have benchmarks?

[00:05:09] Maya: we do internal evals and post a model catalog with per-language BLEU-ish and instruction-following metrics. But we'll run a custom benchmark on your dataset to ensure it's representative. That's part of the SE engagement.

[00:05:22] Marcus: let's talk data sizes — our typical user session includes a 10k token transcript + 5-10k tokens of retrieved docs. So 20k average, spikes to 32k. Memory profile matters.

[00:05:34] Maya: that's a solid profile. we recommend testing at your peak lengths. We'll test throughput and memory under simulated load. Also consider partial retrieval and windowing to reduce effective context if needed.

[00:05:46] Lena: tool-calling again — we need deterministic JSON outputs for ticket creation. can the model be constrained?

[00:05:52] Maya: yes, use function calling with strict schemas, and server-side validation. Some models are better at adhering to structured outputs; we can evaluate which one performs best on your sample prompt set.

[00:06:05] Marcus: are there any gotchas with quantization and tool-calling? we've seen some quantized weights degrade structured output fidelity.

[00:06:15] Maya: that's true — aggressive quantization can affect determinism. Redwood recommends mixed strategies: run evals with quantized candidates and keep the primary inference in a less-aggressive quant mode if structured outputs are critical.

[00:06:30] Sanjay: also worth noting — we can provide model variants as fallbacks; if a quantized variant fails schema checks we can automatically reroute to a more-precise model (at cost).

[00:06:44] Priya: security question — how are logs stored? we need audit logs and token-level access logs and retention controls.

[00:06:51] Maya: Redwood Console offers token and route level cost/latency breakdowns and audit logs. For Private, logs can remain in your VPC. For Hosted we retain minimal logs by default and offer configurable retention. we'll share the doc.

[00:07:05] Marcus: latency numbers — do you have ballpark p95 for 30k tokens on a 70b model on Dedicated?

[00:07:12] Maya: p95 is workload-dependent, but on Dedicated with optimized kernels and batching we typically see 2-5s per 1k tokens at generation time; long-context forward passes can add a few hundred ms. We'll run an exact bench for your mix.

[00:07:26] Lena: I'm concerned about vendor lock if we use Redwood-specific optimizations. how portable are the pipelines?

[00:07:32] Sanjay: Redwood aims to be model-agnostic and provides standard APIs and model catalog. You can pin versions and export model artifacts in supported formats. The infra optimizations live in the runtime but you can migrate models.

[00:07:45] Marcus: ok. what's the typical pilot size for Dedicated — minimum commit?

[00:07:50] Sanjay: Depends on region and GPU type; typical entry is equivalent of 2x A100-class GPUs reserved with burst capacity. We'll include concrete numbers in the pricing spreadsheet.

[00:07:59] Priya: compliance — we will need a penetration test report and SOC2. can you share redacted copies?

[00:08:05] Sanjay: yes, we'll send SOC2, penetration summary, and KMS integration guide.

[00:08:11] Lena: great. use cases: beyond support, we may expand to summarization for compliance, and to auto-classify incoming messages into intents. training / fine-tuning required?

[00:08:21] Maya: for high-precision classification and structured outputs, a small fine-tune or RLHF style alignment on your prompts can help. Redwood supports finetune pipelines for Dedicated/Private customers.

[00:08:33] Marcus: are there rate limits or quotas for Hosted eval?

[00:08:36] Sanjay: Free trials have quotas. For paid Hosted customers we provide adjustable quotas and rate limits; Dedicated gives you reserved throughput.

[00:08:45] Lena: ok, let's get to concrete next steps. we want: 1) SE benchmark on our data; 2) pricing for Hosted vs Dedicated (2 GPU config) and Private baseline; 3) security docs.

[00:08:57] Sanjay: that's what we'll do. Maya — will you run the benchmark?

[00:09:01] Maya: yes, once Marcus uploads the sample dataset (5k labeled examples + 200 long docs), I'll run the shortlist across 3-4 model variants and report accuracy on structured outputs, latency, and token costs by 2027-07-26.

[00:09:13] Marcus: I'll share the dataset by tomorrow EOD and include a short doc describing seq length distribution and traffic patterns.

[00:09:21] Priya: I'll review the security docs but may request a follow-up security call.

[00:09:25] Lena: sounds good. any competitors we should be aware of? we've talked internally about Anthropic and Vertex but cost pushed us toward open model stack.

[00:09:33] Sanjay: makes sense. Redwood's differentiator is production-first runtime and the ability to run same stack across Hosted/Dedicated/Private.

[00:09:41] Marcus: one more thing — function calling throughput. we plan thousands of calls per minute during peak. can you handle that on Dedicated?

[00:09:50] Maya: yes, Dedicated with autoscaling policies and burst capacity can absorb that. We'll include throughput targets in the bench.

[00:10:00] Lena: ok, let's recap and stop — we need the docs and bench artifacts.

[00:10:05] Sanjay: recap: Maya runs benchmark, Marcus uploads data, Sanjay sends pricing and SOC2/KMS docs, Priya reviews security and may schedule follow-up. Next call: technical deep-dive week of Jul 26.

[00:10:18] Lena: thanks everyone, looking forward.

[00:10:20] Sanjay: thanks — we'll follow up with links, sandbox creds, and the benchmark plan.

[00:10:25] End of recording. Note: transcription contains typical mis-hears — product nicknames and internal model names may be slightly off.
